newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU in new stand-off with wheat exporters.
newsitem.headline: EU in new stand-off with wheat exporters.

text.p: The European Commission is engaged in a war of nerves with exporters over the pace of soft wheat exports for the last stretch of the 1996/97 season, grain industry officials said on Wednesday.
Tension has been rising each week as the market finds itself short of licences to cover sales and burst into the open with a market squeeze on licences last week.

Tempers frayed again this week after a Commission official warned that the EU may wrap up exports for the 1996/97 campaign before the traditional end-April deadline, or slow down the rate at which it has been handing out licences.

The remark, contested by other officials, highlighted a possible split within the EU over how fast to keep exporting and alarmed traders who have been scrambling for the last three weeks to secure cover.

Traders are said to be short of some 500,000 tonnes of EU licences and face possible losses on wheat sales to North Africa, having already substantially reduced their bids for wheat subsidies in recent weeks.

The Commission official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters on Monday there was not enough demand on world markets for the EU to continue granting 400,000 tonnes a week in export licences between now and the end of April.
To do so would imply an unrealistic target of 2.4 million tonnes in further export licence approvals with alternative supplies soon becoming more readily available, the official argued.

The official said the EU therefore faced two choices -- to maintain a weekly export pace of 400,000 tonnes, but wrap up exports before end-April, or keep granting wheat exports until the end of April but award fewer licences each week.
Other EU officials said they disagreed with this position, adding the EU would be open for business from mid-May after a three-week pause in EU auctions for various national holidays.
Stakes are high for exporters who need to secure enough licences to cover business to Egypt and particularly Iraq.

The EU has already exported 8.1 million tonnes of soft wheat since the start of the 1996/97 season (July/June). Most exporters acknowledge the EU would find it hard to export an additional two million by the end of the season and put export potential at 1.5 million.
But their margin for manoeuvre has shrunk as EU refunds slide in value and interior prices remain high.

Traders put the net short position at 500,000 tonnes for March. Some have said that for certain deals, with the exception of Iraq, they do not exclude turning to other origins, though this would depend on availability as well as buyers' wishes.
Exporters estimate the EU must grant 400,000 tonnes in export licences to cover politically-sensitive sales of French wheat to Iraq.
Exporters meanwhile face an uphill struggle persuading the Commission to increase the value of export licences to levels that would bail them out of losses put as high as $16 a tonne.
Recent maximum awards at the weekly tender peg EU wheat near $156 per tonne compared with prices in the low $140s on some traders' books.

Exporters said Brussels would do its best to maintain the downward pressure on refunds to help budgets, though it offered the market some relief last week by setting the refund higher than expected to keep the squeeze on licences in check.
EU wheat export subsidies fell to 10.25 Ecus on March 6 from 18.00 Ecus on February 13.
